newsitem.title: USA: Bill proposed to curb liability for U.S. volunteers.
newsitem.headline: Bill proposed to curb liability for U.S. volunteers.

text.p: A bill to limit damage awards against volunteer groups like the Boy Scouts and Little League was introduced in the Senate on Monday amid new pressure to reform liability legislation.

The bill put forward by Missouri Republican John Ashcroft would limit punitive damages against a volunteer organisation or a volunteer to twice the amount of money lost due to injury, or $250,000, whichever was less.

It would also require plaintiffs to prove by clear and convincing evidence that an injury was caused by the defendant's conscious flagrant indifference. This is a higher standard than most civil cases but less than in a criminal case, which requires evidence beyond a reasonable doubt.

Ashcroft said the bill was needed because fear of lawsuits hampered volunteers and volunteer groups from offering their services. "The mere threat of lawsuits increasingly deters volunteers from donating their time and directly restricts the ability to provide important services," he said.

Ashcroft said a study had found that one out of seven nonprofit groups had eliminated one or more programmes and one in six volunteers said they were withholding their services because of fear of exposure to lawsuits. "The understanding that people have been historically willing to help one another is a mainstay of who we are as Americans," he said.
Similar bills limiting product liability awards are pending in the Senate and House.

The Senate Commerce Committee may act on the legislation by late April or early May. Its House counterpart is to hold a hearing Tuesday on how the threat of product liability suits limits access to medical devices.
President Clinton vetoed a bill Congress passed last year to limit product liability damages, saying it went too far in restricting the rights of injury victims to compensation.

Supporters of the bill said Clinton was acting on behalf of trial lawyers, who have been major campaign contributors to his elections. But they failed to get the two-thirds majority needed to override the veto.
The bill is backed by major business groups such as the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers but is opposed by consumer and legal groups.
